## Where This Fits
**W8 made it speak; this week asks who says it spoke well.** W8 wrote TTS as drawing one sample from $P(\mathbf{X} \mid \ell)$ and asked where the decision "which reading" is made. Once samples can be drawn, the four things that decide the experience in a dialogue system — whose voice, in what manner, how to make it better, how to guard against misuse — all share one structure: **a generator, and a judge that scores it.** One question runs through the week: **who is the judge, what can it not see, and does the generator learn exactly that?** (1) **Controllability** adds a condition $\mathbf{c}$ to $P(\mathbf{X} \mid \ell, \mathbf{c})$ — whose voice (a reference recording) and how (a style, an emotion, a natural-language instruction). W8 left one point open — conditioning on a speaker embedding and continuing a prompt differ in what they control and what they leak — and that is this week's first topic; whether the model obeyed is itself answered by a judge (a speaker encoder for similarity, an emotion classifier, or an LLM that understands the instruction). (2) **Post-training** turns the judge into a reward and moves the distribution toward what it likes — the **fourth kind of supervision** previewed in W8: not paired (text, speech) but preferences and scores. (3) **Evaluation** looks at the judges themselves: people (MOS and its statistical traps — the box W8 left closed) and machines (W7's ASR for WER, a speaker encoder for SIM, MOS predictors built on W5's SSL models). (4) **Misuse prevention** replaces the judge by a detector and puts an adversary on the generator's side: anti-spoofing assumes an uncooperative generator, watermarking a cooperative one, and they defend against different things. One regularity holds across all four: **a judge that is optimised against has its blind spots learned** (Goodhart's law). It has already appeared twice without being named: the discriminators $\Phi_j$ of W6 and W8 are judges that live inside training, and the artefacts of a GAN vocoder are what they could not see — which is exactly what today's detectors rely on.

The second thread is **how W8's two paradigms each connect to a reward.** An autoregressive codec LM is already a policy — every token is an action and $\ln \pi_\theta$ is available — so DPO and GRPO carry over from text unchanged. Flow matching, once $\mathbf{X}_0$ is fixed, is a deterministic ODE: there is no probability of "a different action in the same state" to differentiate. Policy gradient needs the ODE replaced by an SDE with the same marginals (the sentence W8 left hanging, picked up this week), or a model that outputs a Gaussian, or no sampling at all — a reward made differentiable with respect to the tokens through Gumbel-softmax (W5's tool returns). We give the structure of all three and derive only DPO and GRPO.

Where the three course-long axes sit this week. **Supervision is the main axis:** the first eight weeks used three kinds (labels, self-supervision, paired synthetic data); this week adds the fourth and asks where rewards come from — cheap and verifiable ones (a frozen ASR for WER, a frozen speaker encoder for SIM), learned ones (a MOS predictor is trained on human ratings, so it inherits their biases and adds out-of-domain failure), and people themselves (a few hundred preference pairs per round are enough to restore prosody; Shin et al. 2026). **Representation:** where "who" and "how" live in W6's tokens — prompt continuation has no bottleneck, so everything in the prompt (channel, noise, emotion, accent) is continued; a speaker embedding is a fixed-size bottleneck that keeps what speaker-verification training asked it to keep; a factorized codec (NaturalSpeech 3) tries to give content, prosody and timbre a subspace each. Where the reward is computed is also a question of representation: on the waveform you must synthesise first, on tokens (DiffRO) you need not. **Latency:** no new cell of the budget is filled this week, but one contrast matters — **post-training changes the weights, not inference**, so the first packet is unchanged, whereas classifier-free guidance (two forward passes per step) and best-of-$N$ reranking (generate $N$ times, let a judge pick; no streaming) keep the judge in the inference path and pay for it in latency. Moving the judge from inference into training is the reason post-training matters in a dialogue system.

Four concrete points on the local-language thread. (1) **The judges themselves are missing or weak for Taiwanese.** Rewards and objective evaluation both rest on ASR, and on Breeze Taigi's own benchmark (2026) the best Taiwanese ASR reaches 30.13% CER (the abstract's figure): used as a reward it teaches that recogniser's errors, not pronunciation. MOS predictors are trained on English ratings (BVCC); detectors of codec-generated speech trained on English do not generalise to tonal South-East Asian languages (SEA-CF, IJCAI-ECAI 2026, as stated in its abstract). (2) **Is tone still in the token?** — the prediction W8 left open. This week adds three pieces of evidence at different levels: k-means units from SSL models lose tone (Osakuade & King, Speech Prosody 2026: the SSL latents encode tone, the quantised units do not do so reliably, and other quantisers do not fix it); Mandarin synthesised from discrete units shows "tone shift" (ToneUnit: right syllable, wrong tone); and an ASR-supervised tokenizer at low frame rate degrades more on Mandarin than on English, which its authors attribute to tone being cut away from the segment (Zhang et al. 2025, measured by ASR error, not by probing tone). **A direct probe of tone in ASR-supervised semantic tokens, or any evidence for Taiwanese, we still have not found** — the claim remains a prediction, but no longer a blank. (3) **Emotion and prosody control move $F_0$, and in our languages $F_0$ is the word** (W2's prediction): "raise the pitch to sound excited" is not a free move in a tone language. This remains a prediction marked *to be verified*; we found no systematic evidence to cite. (4) **Cloning carries the accent along:** a Mandarin prompt reading English, or reading Taiwanese, continues that person's whole way of speaking. Low-resource languages often take the speaker-embedding route instead (for example VoxHakka, a multi-speaker Taiwanese Hakka TTS covering six dialects).

## Learning Objectives
1. Write the three conditioning schemes of zero-shot voice cloning — a speaker embedding, prompt continuation, a factorized codec — as three shapes of $\mathbf{c}$ in $P(\mathbf{X} \mid \ell, \mathbf{c})$; say what each keeps and what each leaks (timbre, prosody, emotion, channel, accent); and design an experiment that measures the leak.
2. Explain three generations of style and emotion control (explicit prosodic parameters, reference encoders and style tokens, natural-language instructions), why emotion is entangled with speaker, text and lexical tone, and why "did it follow the instruction" itself needs a judge.
3. Derive the closed-form optimal policy of KL-constrained reward maximisation, solve it for the reward, and substitute into the Bradley–Terry model to obtain the DPO loss; write GRPO's group-relative advantage and clipped objective and say what it dispenses with; explain how an autoregressive codec LM and a flow-matching model each connect to RL (tokens as actions; an ODE turned into an SDE).
4. Design a reward for TTS (WER, SIM, a MOS predictor, human preferences), predict how the speech degrades when each is optimised alone (reward hacking), and point to the measured evidence in the literature.
5. List the four dimensions of TTS evaluation (intelligibility, naturalness, similarity, controllability) with objective and subjective measures and the conditions under which each fails; design a MOS / CMOS / MUSHRA listening test, state the details that must be reported, explain why ratings are clustered (same rater, same sentence) and why MOS cannot be compared across tests; say how a MOS predictor's training differs from its use.
6. Distinguish the threat models of anti-spoofing and watermarking (who cooperates, who is the adversary); write EER and DCF and use the base rate to compute the precision of one alarm in deployment; and name the known failures of each (unseen generators and neural codecs; resynthesis and speech enhancement).

## Demos
The demos are programs and are published so that you can read them, re-run them, and change them — **you are not required to run anything**. Each folder's `README.md` gives requirements, setup, commands, and what you should see; the index at [`demos/`](https://github.com/hungshinlee/Speech-AI/tree/main/demos) explains the shared environment. Nothing is trained this week: all three demos are inference only.

## References
**Conditioning and voice cloning**
- Jia et al. (11 authors), **Transfer Learning from Speaker Verification to Multispeaker Text-To-Speech Synthesis**, NeurIPS 2018 (arXiv:1806.04558) — the prototype of the speaker-embedding route: an encoder trained for speaker verification, frozen, conditions Tacotron 2
- Snyder, Garcia-Romero, Sell, Povey & Khudanpur, **X-Vectors: Robust DNN Embeddings for Speaker Recognition**, ICASSP 2018, pp. 5329–5333 (DOI 10.1109/ICASSP.2018.8461375) — the embedding used by SpeechT5 in W8's Demo 1; speaker verification itself is W10
- Casanova, Weber, Shulby, Candido Junior, Gölge & Ponti, **YourTTS: Towards Zero-Shot Multi-Speaker TTS and Zero-Shot Voice Conversion for Everyone**, ICML 2022, PMLR 162:2709–2720 (arXiv:2112.02418) — the speaker-embedding route on VITS
- Wang et al. (13 authors), **Neural Codec Language Models are Zero-Shot Text to Speech Synthesizers** (VALL-E), arXiv:2301.02111 (2023; preprint) — the prompt-continuation route (W8); its similarity is computed against the codec-resynthesised prompt
- Le et al. (Meta), **Voicebox: Text-Guided Multilingual Universal Speech Generation at Scale**, NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv:2306.15687) — the source of the SIM-o / SIM-r distinction: similarity against a resynthesised prompt is not comparable across models with different vocoders
- Ju et al. (19 authors), **NaturalSpeech 3: Zero-Shot Speech Synthesis with Factorized Codec and Diffusion Models**, ICML 2024, PMLR 235:22605–22623 (arXiv:2403.03100) — a factorized codec (content / prosody / timbre / detail)
- Wang et al. (11 authors), **An Investigation of Noise Robustness for Flow-Matching-Based Zero-Shot TTS**, Interspeech 2024, pp. 687–691 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2024-1336; arXiv:2406.05699) — generation degrades markedly when the prompt is noisy; training-side remedies
- Lu, Du, Liu, Ai & Ling, **Improving Noise Robustness of LLM-based Zero-shot TTS via Discrete Acoustic Token Denoising**, Interspeech 2025, pp. 2465–2469 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2025-319; arXiv:2505.13830) — opens with the observation that LLM-based zero-shot TTS preserves the prompt's acoustic environment
- Lu, Gu, Wei, Du, Ai & Ling, **DAIEN-TTS: Disentangled Audio Infilling for Environment-Aware Text-to-Speech Synthesis**, ICASSP 2026, pp. 17287–17291 (DOI 10.1109/ICASSP55912.2026.11460953; arXiv:2509.14684) — separate prompts for timbre and for environment, built on F5-TTS

**Evaluation**

- Kirkland, Mehta, Lameris, Henter, Székely & Gustafson, **Stuck in the MOS pit: A critical analysis of MOS test methodology in TTS evaluation**, SSW 2023, pp. 41–47 (DOI 10.21437/SSW.2023-7) — also cited in W8

- Wester, Valentini-Botinhao & Henter, **Are we using enough listeners? No! An empirically-supported critique of Interspeech 2014 TTS evaluations**, Interspeech 2015, pp. 3476–3480 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2015-689)

- Cooper, Huang, Tsao, Wang, Toda & Yamagishi, **A review on subjective and objective evaluation of synthetic speech**, Acoustical Science and Technology 45:161–183, 2024 (DOI 10.1250/ast.e24.12) — the one review to read
- Lo, Fu, Huang, Wang, Yamagishi, Tsao & Wang, **MOSNet: Deep Learning based Objective Assessment for Voice Conversion**, Interspeech 2019, pp. 1541–1545 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2019-2003; arXiv:1904.08352) — an early MOS predictor
- Huang, Cooper, Tsao, Wang, Toda & Yamagishi, **The VoiceMOS Challenge 2022**, Interspeech 2022 (arXiv:2203.11389) — the BVCC data; a main track and an out-of-domain track
- Cooper, Huang, Toda & Yamagishi, **Generalization Ability of MOS Prediction Networks**, ICASSP 2022, pp. 8442–8446 (DOI 10.1109/ICASSP43922.2022.9746395; arXiv:2110.02635)
- Saeki, Xin, Nakata, Koriyama, Takamichi & Saruwatari, **UTMOS: UTokyo-SaruLab System for VoiceMOS Challenge 2022**, Interspeech 2022, pp. 4521–4525 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2022-439; arXiv:2204.02152) — fine-tuned SSL models, listener-dependent training, an ensemble of strong and weak learners
- Huang et al. (8 authors), **The VoiceMOS Challenge 2024: Beyond Speech Quality Prediction**, SLT 2024, pp. 803–810 (DOI 10.1109/SLT61566.2024.10832295; arXiv:2409.07001) — Track 1 predicts MOS "zoomed in" on high-quality systems
- Baba, Nakata, Saito & Saruwatari, **The T05 System for the VoiceMOS Challenge 2024: Transfer Learning from Deep Image Classifier to Naturalness MOS Prediction of High-Quality Synthetic Speech** (UTMOSv2), SLT 2024, pp. 818–824 (DOI 10.1109/SLT61566.2024.10832315; arXiv:2409.09305)
- Minixhofer, Klejch & Bell, **TTSDS — Text-to-Speech Distribution Score**, SLT 2024, pp. 766–773 (DOI 10.1109/SLT61566.2024.10832178; arXiv:2407.12707); and **TTSDS2: Resources and Benchmark for Evaluating Human-Quality Text to Speech Systems**, arXiv:2506.19441 (2025) — evaluation by distributions rather than single utterances
- Varadhan, Thomas, S., Bhooshan & Khapra, **The State Of TTS: A Case Study with Human Fooling Rates**, Interspeech 2025, pp. 2285–2289 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2025-2765; arXiv:2508.04179) — "can it fool a listener" as an alternative to MOS
- Shen et al. (8 authors), **Iterate to Differentiate: Enhancing Discriminability and Reliability in Zero-Shot TTS Evaluation**, Interspeech 2026, pp. 1327–1336 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2026-2414; arXiv:2603.24430) — separating top systems once objective metrics saturate
- **JM3**, the evaluation section of the chapter *Text-to-Speech*
- Other quality predictors: search *NISQA speech quality*, *DNSMOS P.835*, *SpeechLMScore*, *Audiobox Aesthetics*

**Misuse: detection, watermarking, privacy**
- Wang et al. (40 authors), **ASVspoof 2019: A large-scale public database of synthesized, converted and replayed speech**, Computer Speech & Language 64:101114, 2020 (DOI 10.1016/j.csl.2020.101114; arXiv:1911.01601)
- Liu et al. (11 authors), **ASVspoof 2021: Towards Spoofed and Deepfake Speech Detection in the Wild**, IEEE/ACM TASLP 31:2507–2522, 2023 (DOI 10.1109/TASLP.2023.3285283)
- Wang et al. (11 authors), **ASVspoof 5: Evaluation of Spoofing, Deepfake, and Adversarial Attack Detection Using Crowdsourced Speech**, IEEE TASLP 34:2354–2367, 2026 (DOI 10.1109/TASLPRO.2026.3682962; arXiv:2601.03944) — 53 teams; degradation under adversarial attacks and neural codecs; the primary metric moves from EER to DCF (§III-A)
- Kinnunen et al. (11 authors), **Tandem Assessment of Spoofing Countermeasures and Automatic Speaker Verification: Fundamentals**, IEEE/ACM TASLP 28, 2020 (DOI 10.1109/TASLP.2020.3009494; arXiv:2007.05979) — the t-DCF, which scores a detector together with speaker verification (picked up in W10)
- Jung et al. (8 authors), **AASIST: Audio Anti-Spoofing using Integrated Spectro-Temporal Graph Attention Networks**, ICASSP 2022, pp. 6367–6371 (DOI 10.1109/ICASSP43922.2022.9747766; arXiv:2110.01200)
- Tak, Todisco, Wang, Jung, Yamagishi & Evans, **Automatic Speaker Verification Spoofing and Deepfake Detection Using Wav2vec 2.0 and Data Augmentation**, Odyssey 2022, pp. 112–119 (DOI 10.21437/Odyssey.2022-16; arXiv:2202.12233) — an SSL front end
- Wang & Yamagishi, **Spoofed Training Data for Speech Spoofing Countermeasure Can Be Efficiently Created Using Neural Vocoders**, ICASSP 2023 (DOI 10.1109/ICASSP49357.2023.10094779; arXiv:2210.10570) — vocoder-resynthesised real speech as spoofed training data
- Müller, Czempin, Dieckmann, Froghyar & Böttinger, **Does Audio Deepfake Detection Generalize?**, Interspeech 2022, pp. 2783–2787 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2022-108; arXiv:2203.16263) — the In-the-Wild dataset; large degradation on real-world recordings
- Wu, Tseng & Lee, **CodecFake: Enhancing Anti-Spoofing Models Against Deepfake Audios from Codec-Based Speech Synthesis Systems**, Interspeech 2024, pp. 1770–1774 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2024-2093; arXiv:2406.07237); Chen et al. (11 authors), **CodecFake+: Codec-Based Resynthesized Data as a Proxy for Detecting CodecFake Speech**, IEEE TASLP 34:2929–2944, 2026 (DOI 10.1109/TASLPRO.2026.3692291; arXiv:2501.08238) — detectors trained on the usual datasets miss the output of codec-based systems
- Phukan, Girish, Akhtar & Buduru, **Bridging the SEA Gap: An Initial Benchmark for Neural Audio Codec-Synthesized Speech Deepfakes in South-East Asian Languages**, IJCAI-ECAI 2026 (arXiv:2606.15968) — detectors trained on English do not generalise to tonal South-East Asian languages
- Wang, Ge & Yamagishi, **Does Fine-tuning by Reinforcement Learning Improve Generalization in Binary Speech Deepfake Detection?**, Interspeech 2026, pp. 5446–5450 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2026-589; arXiv:2603.02914) — this week's GRPO applied to a detector
- San Roman, Fernandez, Elsahar, Défossez, Furon & Tran, **Proactive Detection of Voice Cloning with Localized Watermarking** (AudioSeal), ICML 2024, PMLR 235:43180–43196 (arXiv:2401.17264) — a generator and a detector trained jointly; detection at the level of single samples; the detector's weights should stay confidential (§6)
- Chen, Wu, Liu, Liu, Du & Wei, **WavMark: Watermarking for Audio Generation**, arXiv:2308.12770 (2023; preprint)
- Liu, Guo, Jiang, Wang & Gong, **AudioMarkBench: Benchmarking Robustness of Audio Watermarking**, NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks (arXiv:2406.06979) — three watermarks, 15 perturbations, removal and forgery under no-box, black-box and white-box access
- Chen et al. (8 authors, National Taiwan University), **Latent-Mark: An Audio Watermark Robust to Neural Codec Compression**, Interspeech 2026, pp. 3052–3061 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2026-1979; arXiv:2603.05310) — a watermark placed in the codec's latent space
- Zhong et al. (7 authors), **The Vulnerability of Neural Audio Watermarks under Speech Enhancement**, arXiv:2609.29040 (2026; preprint) — speech enhancement as a removal attack, compared with codec and vocoder resynthesis

- Zhu, Cao, Jin, Guo, Mo, Xue & Song, **KeyBound: Keyed and Host-Bound Learned Audio Watermarking for Speech Provenance**, arXiv:2609.26235 (2026; a preprint, not peer-reviewed) — its Appendix A.1 re-measures the false-positive rate on unmarked audio after every attack, with AudioSeal through EnCodec as one of the baselines
- Tomashenko et al. (14 authors), **The VoicePrivacy 2020 Challenge: Results and findings**, Computer Speech & Language 74:101362, 2022 (DOI 10.1016/j.csl.2022.101362) — the task and metrics of voice anonymisation
- Yu, Zhai & Zhang, **AntiFake: Using Adversarial Audio to Prevent Unauthorized Speech Synthesis**, ACM CCS 2023, pp. 460–474 (DOI 10.1145/3576915.3623209) — a proactive defence: perturb your own recordings so that cloning fails

**Local languages and tone**
- Osakuade & King, **Lexical Tone is Hard to Quantize: Probing Discrete Speech Units in Mandarin and Yorùbá**, Speech Prosody 2026, pp. 38–42 (DOI 10.21437/SpeechProsody.2026-8; arXiv:2604.07467); and **Do Discrete Self-Supervised Representations of Speech Capture Tone Distinctions?**, arXiv:2410.19935 (2024; preprint) — SSL latents encode tone; quantised units do not do so reliably
- Tao, Tan, Yeung, Chen & Lee, **ToneUnit: A Speech Discretization Approach for Tonal Language Speech Synthesis**, arXiv:2406.08989 (2024; preprint) — "tone shift" in Mandarin synthesised from discrete units, and tone labels as CTC supervision
- Zhang et al. (10 authors), **Impact of Frame Rates on Speech Tokenizer: A Case Study on Mandarin and English**, arXiv:2505.17076 (2025; preprint) — an ASR-supervised tokenizer loses more on Mandarin than on English as the frame rate drops (measured by recognition error, not by probing tone)
- Lan et al. (8 authors), **Breeze Taigi: Benchmarks and Models for Taiwanese Hokkien Speech Recognition and Synthesis**, arXiv:2603.19259 (2026; preprint) — a benchmark for Taiwanese ASR and TTS, with CER as the standard metric
- Chen, Lee & Chang, **VoxHakka: A Dialectally Diverse Multi-speaker Text-to-Speech System for Taiwanese Hakka**, O-COCOSDA 2024 (DOI 10.1109/O-COCOSDA64382.2024.10800327; arXiv:2409.01548) — a multi-speaker Hakka TTS covering six dialects
- Synthetic-speech detection and MOS prediction for Taiwanese and Hakka: search *Taiwanese Hokkien deepfake detection*, *MOS prediction low-resource languages*, *cross-lingual speech quality prediction*
